thread.title: Stanek brings leadership focus as Cardinals seek consistency from new reliever
thread.title_full: Stanek brings leadership focus as Cardinals seek consistency from new reliever

author: K. J. Gordon
title: Stanek brings leadership focus as Cardinals seek consistency from new reliever
text:
Before signing reliever Ryne Stanek to a one-year contract worth $3.5 million, with a $6 million club option for 2027, the St. Louis Cardinals held a Zoom meeting with him. The team emphasized that his role would go beyond pitching in high-pressure situations; they wanted him to serve as a positive influence on younger relief pitchers such as Gordon Graceffo, Chris Roycroft, and Matt Svanson.
Stanek, who is 34 years old, reflected on his early career experiences with the Tampa Bay Rays when veteran Tommy Hunter mentored him. “As a young guy, he would say, ‘Come to dinner. We are going to do this,’” Stanek recalled. “He really didn’t give me a choice. It was like he wanted me involved. His thought was, ‘This is how you take care of the young guys.’ You are supposed to take them out to dinner. You are supposed to take them to do things. Show them what it means to be a pro. Not only that, Tommy was really good at taking care of people.”
Nearly ten years later, Stanek is now providing similar guidance within the Cardinals’ bullpen. Manager Oliver Marmol has been impressed by Stanek’s approach since joining the team.
“Outside of his skill set, he has done a nice job bringing this group together. This is part of the Zoom we had with him prior to signing,” Marmol said. “His personality is perfect. He does a really nice job of making the entire room feel like they belong.”
While Stanek’s leadership has been well received by teammates and coaches alike, the Cardinals are also looking for consistent performance from him on the mound this season. Last year during his time with the New York Mets, he struggled after the All-Star break—allowing 18 runs (17 earned) over 24 1/3 innings in 28 games and posting a 6.29 ERA as the Mets missed postseason play.
Stanek attributed those difficulties to losing command of his split-finger fastball: “Losing your best weapon is never a recipe for success,” he said. “I tried to get it back to normal and then went in a couple of wrong directions. By the time I found it again, the season was over.”
Now working closely with Cardinals pitching coach Dusty Blake, Stanek believes focusing on trusting himself and being more assertive on the mound will help improve results moving forward.
“A lot of it comes from trust and how things are feeling and all of these things,” Stanek said. “It’s about trusting yourself and not overthinking things while on the mound.”
